---
title: "Combining and joining"
---

Often, as data journalists, we're looking at data across time or at data stored in multiple tables. And to do that, we need to often need to merge that data together.

Depending on what we have, we may just need to stack data on top of each other to make new data. If we have 2019 data and 2018 data and we want that to be one file, we stack them. If we have a dataset of cows in counties and a dataset of populations in county, we're going to join those two together on the county -- the common element.

Let's explore.

## Combining data (stacking)

Every school year, the Maryland Department of Health asks every public and private school to report how many of its kindergarteners are fully vaccinated against diseases like measles, polio and whooping cough, and how many have a medical or religious exemption from the state's vaccination requirements. The department publishes the results as a PDF table, one row for each of Maryland's 23 counties plus Baltimore City. (In the chapter on PDFs, you'll learn how to get data like this out of PDFs.)

Let's say that we have that kindergarten immunization data from five different school years in five different files. They have the same record layout and the same number of counties (plus Baltimore City). We can combine them into a single dataframe.

Let's do what we need to import them properly. I've merged it all into one step for each of the datasets.

```{r}
#| output: false
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
kindergarten_2018 <- read_csv("data/md_kindergarten_immunization_2018.csv")
kindergarten_2019 <- read_csv("data/md_kindergarten_immunization_2019.csv")
kindergarten_2020 <- read_csv("data/md_kindergarten_immunization_2020.csv")
kindergarten_2021 <- read_csv("data/md_kindergarten_immunization_2021.csv")
kindergarten_2023 <- read_csv("data/md_kindergarten_immunization_2023.csv")
```

All of these datasets have the same number of columns, all with the same names (or so it seems), so if we want to merge them together to compare them over time, we need to stack them together. The verb here, in R, is `bind_rows`. You tell the function what you want to combine and it does it, assuming that you've got column names in common containing identically formatted data.

Since we have five dataframes, we're going to need to pass them as a list, meaning they'll be enclosed inside the `list` function.

```{r}
kindergarten_combined <- bind_rows(list(kindergarten_2018, kindergarten_2019, kindergarten_2020, kindergarten_2021, kindergarten_2023))
```

And boom, like that, we have 120 rows of data together instead of five dataframes. But look closely at the columns:

```{r}
glimpse(kindergarten_combined)
```

We have 13 columns, not 12. There's an `ENROLLED` column *and* an `Enrolled` column. The 2021 file spelled that column name differently, and `bind_rows` matches columns by their exact names -- including whether letters are upper or lower case. So it made a new column for the 2021 values and filled in NA for every other year, and vice versa. This is a common problem when you combine files that were created by different people or at different times.

The fix is to make the names match *before* we combine. We can use `rename`, which takes the new name first and the old name second:

```{r}
kindergarten_2021 <- kindergarten_2021 |> rename(ENROLLED = Enrolled)

kindergarten_combined <- bind_rows(list(kindergarten_2018, kindergarten_2019, kindergarten_2020, kindergarten_2021, kindergarten_2023))

glimpse(kindergarten_combined)
```

Now we have 120 rows and 12 columns. We can ask more interesting questions, like how a county's religious exemption rate has changed over time:

```{r}
kindergarten_combined |>
  filter(COUNTY == "Cecil") |>
  select(SCHOOL_YEAR, ENROLLED, RELIGIOUS_EXEMPT)
```

Notice anything odd about the 2020-2021 school year? Look at it for a few other counties. That was the first school year of the COVID-19 pandemic, when many schools were teaching remotely and some reported far fewer kindergarteners than usual -- or none at all. Stacking data from several years together makes problems like that easier to spot.

There are plenty of uses for `bind_rows`: any regularly updated data that comes in the same format like disease reports or hospital inspections or grant recipients. Or vaccination rates.

## Joining data

More complicated is when you have two separate tables that are connected by a common element or elements. But there's a verb for that, too: `join`.

Let's start by reading in some Maryland 2020 county population data:

```{r}
maryland_population <- read_csv('data/maryland_population_2020.csv')
```

One of the columns we have is called `COUNTY`, which is what we have in our kindergarten_2023 dataframe.

To put the Maryland population data and kindergarten immunization data together, we need to use something called a join. There are different kinds of joins. It's better if you think of two tables sitting next to each other. A `left_join` takes all the records from the left table and only the records that match in the right one. A `right_join` does the same thing. An `inner_join` takes only the records where they are equal. There's one other join -- a `full_join` which returns all rows of both, regardless of if there's a match -- but I've never once had a use for a full join.

In the best-case scenario, the two tables we want to join share a common column. In this case, both of our tables have a column called `COUNTY` that has the same characteristics: values in both look identical, including how they distinguish Baltimore City from Baltimore County, and how they spell Prince George's, Queen Anne's and St. Mary's. This is important, because joins work on *exact matches*. If one file said "Saint Mary's" and the other said "St. Mary's", they wouldn't match.

We can do this join multiple ways and get a similar result. We can put the population file on the left and the kindergarten data on the right and use a left join to get them all together. And we use `join_by()` to join by the correct column. I'm going to count the rows at the end. The reason I'm doing this is important: **Rule 1 in joining data is having an idea of what you are expecting to get**. So with a left join with population on the left, I have 24 rows, so I expect to get 24 rows when I'm done.

```{r}
maryland_population |> left_join(kindergarten_2023, join_by(COUNTY)) |> nrow()
```

Remove the nrow and run it again for yourself. By default, `dplyr` will do a "natural" join, where it'll match all the matching columns in both tables. So if we take out the `join_by`, it'll use all the common columns between the tables. That may not be right in every instance but let's try it. If it works, we should get 24 rows.

```{r}
maryland_population |> left_join(kindergarten_2023)
```

Since we only have one column in common between the two tables, the join only used that column. And we got the same answer. If we had more columns in common, you could see in your results columns with .x and .y after them - that's a sign of duplicative columns between two tables, and you may decide you don't need both moving forward.

Let's save our joined data to a new dataframe.

```{r}
maryland_population_with_kindergarten <- maryland_population |> left_join(kindergarten_2023)
```

Now, with our joined data, we can answer questions in a more useful way. But joins can do even more than just bring data together; they can include additional data to enable you to ask more sophisticated questions. Right now we have kindergarten vaccination rates and total population. But we can do more.

Let's try adding more Maryland demographic data to the mix. Using a file describing the 18-and-over population from [the state's data catalog](https://planning.maryland.gov/MSDC/Pages/census/Census2020/pL_2020redistricting.aspx), we can read it into R:

```{r}
maryland_demographics <- read_csv('data/maryland_demographics.csv')
```

Again, we can use a `left_join` to make our demographic data available. This time we'll need to specify the two fields to join because they do not have identical names. We'll use `COUNTY` from our population data and `NAME` from the demographic data, and the order matters - the first column is from the dataframe you name *first*.

```{r}
maryland_population_with_kindergarten_and_demographics <- maryland_population_with_kindergarten |> left_join(maryland_demographics, join_by(COUNTY==NAME))
```

Now we've got population data, demographic data and kindergarten vaccination data by county. That means we can draw from all three in asking our questions. The kindergarten data only gives us exemption *rates* -- the percentage of surveyed kindergarteners with an exemption. Rates are useful for comparing places of different sizes, but readers also want to know how many children we're talking about. Since we know how many students were surveyed, we can estimate the number of religious exemptions in each county. And since the demographic data tells us how many residents are 18 and over, we can figure out how many are under 18, too.

We can get this by using mutate and arrange:

```{r}
maryland_population_with_kindergarten_and_demographics |>
  mutate(
    religious_exemptions = round(SURVEYED * RELIGIOUS_EXEMPT / 100),
    pop_under_18 = POP2020 - pop_18_over,
    exemptions_per_10k_children = religious_exemptions / pop_under_18 * 10000
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(religious_exemptions)) |>
  select(COUNTY, religious_exemptions, RELIGIOUS_EXEMPT, exemptions_per_10k_children)
```

The biggest jurisdictions -- Baltimore City, Montgomery and Prince George's -- have the most kindergarteners with religious exemptions, which isn't surprising. But Baltimore City's exemptions per 10,000 children is about twice Montgomery County's. And look at Harford County: it has far fewer exemptions than the big jurisdictions, but one of the highest rates.

Let's change that to look at which counties have the largest share of their population under 18, and how their exemption rates compare:

```{r}
maryland_population_with_kindergarten_and_demographics |>
  mutate(pct_under_18 = (POP2020 - pop_18_over) / POP2020 * 100) |>
  arrange(desc(pct_under_18)) |>
  select(COUNTY, pct_under_18, RELIGIOUS_EXEMPT, MEDICAL_EXEMPT)
```

Here, Howard, St. Mary's and Charles counties stand out as the places with the largest share of children. Their religious exemption rates are close to the statewide rate of 1.54%, which suggests that having a lot of children isn't, by itself, related to exemption rates.

Sometimes joins look like they should work but don't. Often this is due to the two columns you're joining on having different data types: joining a <chr> column to a <dbl> column, for example. Let's walk through an example of that using some demographic data by zip code.

```{r}
maryland_zcta <- read_csv('data/maryland_zcta.csv')
glimpse(maryland_zcta)
```

You can see that ZCTA5N, the column representing the Zip Code Tabulation Area, is a numeric column. But should it be? Do we ever want to know the average zip code in Maryland? Zip codes and ZCTAs look like numbers but really are character columns. Let's change that so that we can be sure to join them correctly with other data where the zip codes are not numbers. We'll use `mutate`:

```{r}
maryland_zcta <- maryland_zcta |> mutate(across(ZCTA5N, as.character))
```

What's happening here is that we're telling R to take all of the values in the ZCTA5N column and make them "as.character". If we wanted to change a column to numeric, we'd do "as.numeric". When you join two dataframes, the join columns *must* be the same datatype.

Joining datasets allows you to expand the range and sophistication of questions you're able to ask. It is one of the most powerful tools in a journalist's toolkit.
